title: Prefix sums & binary search
overview: This module makes two slow patterns fast. Prefix sums answer range-sum queries in O(1) after one O(n) pass, and binary search finds a value in a sorted array in O(log n) instead of O(n). The practice day applies both ideas: running sums, equilibrium index, search queries and an O(1) formula.

concepts.explain: `pre[i]` stores the sum of the first `i` elements. You build it once with `pre[i] = pre[i-1] + a[i]`.
The sum of `a[l..r]` is everything up to `r` minus everything before `l`: `pre[r] - pre[l-1]`. Using 1-based arrays with `pre[0] = 0` removes the special case for `l = 1`.
Many values up to 10^9 added together quickly pass the `int` limit (about 2.1 * 10^9), so sums should be `long long`.
In a sorted array, look at the middle. If it is too small, throw away the left half; if too big, throw away the right half. Each step halves the range, so it takes O(log n) steps.
concepts.snippet:
int mid = (l + r) / 2;
if(a[mid] < x) l = mid + 1; else r = mid - 1;

concepts.term: Sort first, then search many times
concepts.explain: Sorting costs O(n log n) once; after that, each of the `q` queries costs O(log n). That beats O(n*q) linear search for many queries.
If you know the total, the right-side sum at index `i` is `total - leftSum - a[i]`, so one pass finds an equilibrium index.

files.title: Range sum query (1-based brute force)

problem.name: Codeforces group - Y. Range sum query

files.what: Stores the array 1-based and loops from `l` to `r` for every query. Simple and correct, but O(n) per query.
steps: Make `vector<int> a(n+1)` and read into `a[1..n]` so indexes match the problem.
For each query, add `a[l]` through `a[r]` into `sum`.
files.input_note: n q, the array, then q lines of l r.
files.output_note: `12`, `7`, `15`, matching the judge's second sample (5+5+2, 5+2, all four).
files.watch_out: Gets TLE on large tests and `int sum` can overflow. The prefix-sum version below is the intended solution.

check.q: What does storing the array from index 1 buy you here?
check.a: Query indexes can be used directly without subtracting 1.

files.title: Range sum query with prefix sums

problem.name: Codeforces group - Y. Range sum query

files.what: Builds a `long long` prefix-sum array once, then answers each query as `prefixSum[r] - prefixSum[l-1]` in O(1).
steps: Read the array 1-based into `vector<long long> a(n+1)`.
Set `prefixSum[1] = a[1]` and, for `i` from 2, `prefixSum[i] = prefixSum[i-1] + a[i]`.
For a query with `l == 1` the answer is `prefixSum[r]`.
files.input_note: n q, the array, then q lines of l r.
files.output_note: The file does not compile, so there is no output. Once fixed, it prints `12`, `18`, `28` (the judge's first sample).
files.watch_out: Compile error: `sum` is declared twice (`long long int sum = 0;` and then `int sum;`). Delete the `int sum;` line. Keeping the `int` version would also overflow on big sums.

check.q: With prefix sums 6 10 12 19 21 28, what is the sum of positions 3 to 6?

files.title: Linear search vs binary search
files.what: Looks for `val` first with a linear scan (O(n)) and then with binary search (O(log n)) on an array assumed to be sorted.
steps: Linear search: check each `a[i]`; set `flag = 1` and stop when found. Print `found` or `not found`.
Binary search: keep a window `l..r`, starting at `0..n-1`.
Compute `mid`; if `a[mid] == val` set `flag2` and stop.
If `a[mid] < val` the answer can only be to the right, so `l = mid + 1`; otherwise `r = mid - 1`.
The loop stops when the window is empty (`l > r`).
files.complexity: Linear O(n) · Binary O(log n) · Space O(n)
files.input_note: n, a sorted array, then the value to find.
files.output_note: Only one line, `found`, from the linear search. The binary-search result is computed but never printed.
files.watch_out: `flag2` is never printed. Add `cout << (flag2 ? "found" : "not found") << endl;` after the loop. Binary search is only correct on a sorted array; sort first if unsure.

check.q: Searching for 7 in `1 3 5 7 9`, which indexes does binary search check?
check.a: mid = 2 (value 5, too small, so l = 3), then mid = 3 (value 7, found).

files.title: Many search queries, brute force
files.what: Answers `q` queries by scanning the whole array each time.
steps: For each query `x`, scan `a[0..n-1]` and set `flag` if found.
files.input_note: n q, the array (any order), then q values.
files.output_note: `found`, `not found`, `found`: 1 and 8 are in the array, 5 is not.
files.watch_out: With n and q up to 10^5 this is too slow (TLE). See the efficient version.

check.q: Does this version need the array to be sorted?
check.a: No. A linear scan works on any order.

files.title: Many search queries, sort + binary search
files.what: Sorts the array once, then answers every query with binary search.
steps: Read the array and call `sort(a, a+n)`.
While `l <= r`: compare `a[mid]` with `x` and move `l` or `r` past `mid`.
Print `found` if the loop hit `x`, else `not found`.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n + q log n) · Space O(n)
files.input_note: Same input as the brute-force version.
files.output_note: Same answers, `found`, `not found`, `found`, but each query now takes only about 3 steps.

check.q: Why is sorting once worth it here?
check.a: The O(n log n) sort is paid once, and then each of the q queries drops from O(n) to O(log n).

files.title: Running sum of an array
files.what: Builds the running (prefix) sum: each position holds the sum of all elements up to it.
files.watch_out: The task asks for a function, but the code is all in `main`. Crashes if `n` is 0 because of `nums[0]`.

check.q: Why reuse `runningSum[i-1]` instead of summing from scratch?
check.a: It turns O(n^2) work into O(n), since each step only adds one new number.

files.title: Equilibrium index (total minus left)
files.what: Finds the first index where the sum on its left equals the sum on its right, using the total sum and a running left sum.
steps: If they are equal, print `i` and stop.
Otherwise add `a[i]` to `leftSum` and move on.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) for the input
files.output_note: `3`: left of index 3 is -7+1+5 = -1, right is -4+3+0 = -1.

check.q: For `1 2 3 3`, what does the program print?

files.title: Equilibrium index with a prefix array
files.what: Same task, but tries to precompute a prefix array and get left and right sums from it.
steps: For each `i`, left sum is `prefixSum[i-1]` (0 when `i` is 0).
Print the first `i` where they match, else `-1`.
files.output_note: No output: the program crashes (heap corruption) while building the prefix array.
files.watch_out: The loop condition is `i<<n` (bit shift) instead of `i<n`. `i<<n` is non-zero for every `i >= 1`, so the loop writes far past the vector and crashes. Also `prefixSum[0]` should be `a[0]`, not 0. Fix: `prefixSum[0] = a[0]; for(int i=1; i<n; i++)`.

check.q: With a correct prefix array, what is the right sum at index `i`?

files.title: Search query with a binarySearch function
files.what: Sorts the vector and answers each query with a separate `binarySearch` function that returns true or false.
steps: Inside, shrink `left..right` around `mid` until found (return true) or empty (return false).
files.complexity: Time O(n log n + q*n) as written (see Watch out); O((n + q) log n) with a reference · Space O(n)
files.input_note: n, the array, q, then q values.
files.watch_out: `binarySearch(vector<int> arr, ...)` takes the vector by value, so every call copies all n elements (O(n)). Write `const vector<int>& arr` to keep each query O(log n).

check.q: What does the function return when `left` passes `right`?
check.a: false: the search window is empty, so the target is not present.

files.title: Summation from 1 to N in O(1)

problem.name: Codeforces group - G. Summation from 1 to N

files.what: Uses the formula `n*(n+1)/2` with `long long` to print the sum instantly.
files.output_note: `5000050000`, larger than an `int` can hold, which is why `long long` is used.

check.q: What would go wrong with `int n` for N = 100000?
check.a: `n * (n + 1)` is about 10^10, which overflows a 32-bit int.

recap: Prefix sums: build once in O(n), then each range sum is `pre[r] - pre[l-1]` in O(1).
Use 1-based arrays with `pre[0] = 0` to avoid the `l == 1` special case.
Binary search needs a sorted array and halves the window each step: O(log n).
Many queries: sort once, then binary search each one.
Pass big vectors to functions by reference to avoid copying.

check_yourself.q: For `a = 3 1 4 1 5` (1-based), what is the prefix array and the sum of positions 2..4?
How many steps does binary search need at most for 1,000,000 sorted elements?
Why does `(l + r) / 2` sometimes get written as `l + (r - l) / 2`?
check_yourself.a: For huge indexes, `l + r` can overflow `int`; the second form avoids that.

body: A shop writes down its takings each day. Six days: 6, 4, 2, 7, 2, 7. Someone asks how much came in over days 1 to 3, and you add them up: 12. Then days 3 to 6: 2 + 7 + 2 + 7 = 18. Then days 1 to 6. Every question sends you back over the list.

That is fine for six days and three questions. The real version has 100000 days and 100000 questions, and adding up to 100000 numbers per question is O(n) each time, O(n*q) altogether - about 10^10 steps, with no hope of finishing in 1 second.
A shopkeeper would not work that way either. They would keep a running total: 6 after day 1, 10 after day 2, 12 after day 3, and so on. One walk down the list, one line of the book per day.

Now any stretch of days is a subtraction. Days 3 to 6 is everything up to day 6 minus everything before day 3: `pre[6] - pre[2]` = 28 - 10 = 18. Check it by hand: 2 + 7 + 2 + 7 = 18. Days 1 to 3 is `pre[3] - pre[0]` = 12 - 0 = 12, and that is why it pays to store the array from index 1 with `pre[0] = 0` - then `l = 1` needs no special case.

**What is new.** One walk over the data, paid for once, turns every later question into a single subtraction: O(n) to build, O(1) per query. Keep the totals in `long long`, because 100000 values of up to 10^9 pass the `int` limit of about 2.1 * 10^9 long before the end.

The second idea starts with a phone book. To find "Rahman" you do not begin at page one; you open somewhere in the middle, see that you are past the R's, and drop the whole second half. It is the game of guessing a number between 1 and 100: guess 50, hear "too high", and fifty possibilities are gone at once.

It only works because the pages are in order. In code you keep a window `lo..hi`, look at the middle `mid`, and throw away the half that cannot hold the value. Here is the search for 31 in a sorted array of eight numbers:
Three looks, where a linear search would have compared seven elements before reaching it.
intro.trace:
a:    3   8  12  15  19  23  31  40
idx   0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7
looking for 31

lo  hi  mid  a[mid]  what happens
 0   7    3      15  too small, lo = 4
 4   7    5      23  too small, lo = 6
 6   7    6      31  found at index 6

body: Each step halves the window, so the work is O(log n): at most about 20 looks in a million elements, 30 in a billion. The price is that the array must be sorted - on an unsorted array the middle element tells you nothing about which half to keep.

So when there are many searches you sort once and then search fast: O(n log n) for the sort plus O(log n) for each of the `q` queries, against O(n) per query for a linear scan. With `n` and `q` both 100000 that is roughly 3.4 million steps instead of 10^10.

**Two more places the running total turns up.** An equilibrium index is a position where everything to its left adds up to the same as everything to its right; knowing the total, the right side is `total - leftSum - a[i]`, so one pass finds it. And the sum 1 + 2 + ... + n needs no loop at all: `n * (n + 1) / 2` answers in O(1).
The programs below show the important ones twice - the slow version first, then the fast one - so you can see exactly which loop disappeared.
